extracted.intended_audience: political thinkers, legislators, and educated public interested in constitutional design and revolutionary critique
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and normative principles for judging the composition, legitimacy, and prudence of governments and assemblies, especially in the context of revolutionary change. Focuses on representation, property, experience, institutional restraints, and the dangers of professional or demagogic dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative composition should reflect varied distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons, without shutting its doors to any merit in any class, is, by the sure operation of adequate causes, filled with everything illustrious in rank, in descent, in hereditary and in acquired opulence, in cultivated talents, in military, civil, naval, and politic distinction, that the country can afford.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation ought to include a mix of ranks, heredity, acquired wealth, cultivated talents, and distinctions across military, civil, naval, and political spheres. Diversity across social orders prevents narrowness of perspective and strengthens governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid professional preponderance in legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: When men are too much confined to professional and faculty habits... they are rather disabled than qualified for whatever depends on the knowledge of mankind, on experience in mixed affairs, on a comprehensive, connected view of the various... interests which go to the formation of that multifarious thing called a State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legislature dominated by one profession (e.g., lawyers) will lack the breadth required for complex statecraft; selection mechanisms should prevent overrepresentation of narrow professional classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional restraints and respected usages as necessary controls
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons, circumscribed and shut in by the immovable barriers of laws, usages, positive rules of doctrine and practice, counterpoised by the House of Lords, and every moment of its existence at the discretion of the crown... The National Assembly... has no fundamental law, no strict convention, no respected usage to restrain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power must be bounded by laws, conventions, counterbalancing bodies, and institutional checks; absence of entrenched restraints enables unchecked and potentially destructive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives must have aptitude and worldly experience
rubrics_metrics.description: That election was so contrived as to send a very large proportion of mere country curates... men who never had seen the state so much as in a picture; men who knew nothing of the world beyond the bounds of an obscure village.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral design should favor candidates with broad experience and understanding of public affairs rather than sending those ignorant of state matters; avoid electing representatives motivated by envy or hopes of plunder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent remuneration of followers by public plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: In the spoil and humiliation of their own order these individuals would possess a sure fund for the pay of their new followers... To squander away the objects which made the happiness of their fellows would be to them no sacrifice at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against leaders who use confiscation or redistribution of property to pay or bind followers; ensure incentives and institutional constraints that prevent looting of public or private property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders of change should have long views and public talents
rubrics_metrics.description: Other revolutions have been conducted by persons who... sanctified their ambition by advancing the dignity of the people whose peace they troubled. They had long views. They aimed at the rule, not at the destruction of their country. They were men of great civil and great military talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers or revolutionaries ought to be judged by whether they possess statesmanship and seek to elevate national dignity and improvement rather than mere personal or destructive aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the moral 'mind' and institutions of the country
rubrics_metrics.description: France... recovered and emerged from the longest and most dreadful civil war... Because, among all their massacres, they had not slain the mind in their country. A conscious dignity, a noble pride... was not extinguished. The organs also of the state, however shattered, existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain honors, distinctions, and institutional organs even amid upheaval so the nation can recover; wholesale destruction of moral and institutional frameworks impedes future restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow openness of opportunity, but not equal indifference to fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything ought to be open,—but not indifferently to every man. No rotation, no appointment by lot... can be generally good in a government conversant in extensive objects; because they have no tendency... to select the man with a view to the duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access to offices should be open in principle, but appointments must consider merit, probatory testing, and suitability rather than pure egalitarian devices like lot or enforced rotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must express ability as well as property
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is a due and adequate representation of a state, that does not represent its ability, as well as its property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative bodies should represent both the nation's capacities (talent, ability) and its property interests; mere population numbers are insufficient for adequate political representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property should be protected via concentrated representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic essence of property... is to be unequal. The great masses, therefore, which excite envy, and tempt rapacity, must be put out of the possibility of danger. Then they form a natural rampart about the lesser properties in all their gradations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because property tends to concentrate, its defensive power comes from being represented in large masses (e.g., hereditary estates, upper chamber); protecting major holders protects smaller proprietors as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuation of family property is valuable to society
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of perpetuating our property in our families is one of the most valuable and interesting circumstances belonging to it, and that which tends the most to the perpetuation of society itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and institutional mechanisms that allow transmission of property across generations (e.g., hereditary peers) serve social stability and align private incentive with public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject facile leveling that destroys natural order
rubrics_metrics.description: Believe me, Sir, those who attempt to level never equalize. In all societies consisting of various descriptions of citizens, some description must be uppermost. The levellers, therefore, only change and pervert the natural order of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies aiming to flatten social distinctions risk destabilizing society; reforms should not confuse 'leveling' with genuine equalization and must respect functional hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy is not solely a function of popular representation
rubrics_metrics.description: They value themselves on being systematic... that a representation chosen chiefly by the Treasury... is a 'semblance'... They think the House of Commons... a 'shadow'... Yet the Revolution itself... wants a title; the Revolution is built... upon a basis not more solid than our present formalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question doctrines that reduce all government legitimacy to a single criterion (pure popular choice); historical legitimacy, precedent, and constitutional arrangements also matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: No man should be judge in his own cause
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the first motives to civil society... is, that no man should be judge in his own cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional impartiality and separation of adjudicative power are foundational: design governance to prevent self-judgment and conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government exists to provide for human wants and restrain passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Government is a contrivance of human wisdom to provide for human wants. Men have a right that these wants should be provided for by this wisdom... Society requires... that the passions of individuals should be subjected... by a power out of themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design government powers to enable provision of collective needs and to moderate destructive passions; rights should be balanced with social restraints necessary for order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical experience should guide constitutional engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of constructing a commonwealth... is, like every other experimental science, not to be taught a priori... it requires experience, and even more experience than any person can gain in his whole life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional reform should be cautious, empirically informed, and based on models of approved utility rather than purely theoretical abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract rights must be tempered by convention and practical limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: These metaphysic rights entering into common life... are, by the laws of Nature, refracted from their straight line... The moment you abate anything from the full rights of men... the whole organization of government becomes a consideration of convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that natural or abstract rights will be modified in application by social conventions and the needs of civil society; debates about rights should account for practical consequences and necessary limits.
